module_title: Law of Limitation: Foundational Concepts & Maxims
introduction: This foundational level explores the concept of 'Limitation'—the statutorily prescribed time limit within which a person must approach the court to enforce a right. It covers the underlying philosophy of the Limitation Act, 1963, and the absolute mandate of Section 3.

core_concepts.title: The Philosophy of Limitation
core_concepts.description:
The Limitation Act is built upon two fundamental public policy maxims:
1. Interest reipublicae ut sit finis litium: 'It is in the interest of the State that there should be an end to litigation.' Society requires certainty and peace; old, stale claims should not be allowed to hang over people's heads forever.
2. Vigilantibus non dormientibus jura subveniunt: 'The law assists those who are vigilant, not those who sleep over their rights.' If you ignore your rights for an unreasonable amount of time, the court will refuse to help you.

core_concepts.title: The General Rule: Bars Remedy, Not the Right
core_concepts.description:
The most fundamental concept in Limitation law: The Act only bars the *judicial remedy*, it does NOT extinguish the underlying *right*.
- Example: A owes B ₹10,000. The limitation period to sue for recovery is 3 years. If B doesn't sue within 3 years, the court will dismiss B's lawsuit (remedy is barred). However, the debt (A's legal obligation to pay) still exists. If A voluntarily pays B after 4 years, A cannot ask for a refund claiming the debt was dead. B still had the 'right' to receive it.

core_concepts.title: Bar of Limitation (Section 3)
core_concepts.description:
The absolute, non-negotiable hammer of the Act.
- The Rule: Subject to the provisions contained in Sections 4 to 24, EVERY suit instituted, appeal preferred, and application made after the prescribed period **shall be dismissed**, ALTHOUGH limitation has not been set up as a defense.
- Suo Motu Duty: The judge is legally bound to dismiss a time-barred case on their own (*suo motu*), even if the defendant forgets to mention that the case is filed late.

core_concepts.title: Limitation vs. Laches
core_concepts.description:
A classic distinction:
- Limitation: A strict statutory time limit fixed by the Limitation Act (e.g., exactly 3 years). It applies strictly to civil suits, appeals, and applications.
- Laches: An equitable doctrine meaning 'unreasonable delay'. It applies to Constitutional Writ Petitions (like Article 32 or 226) where there is no fixed statutory time limit, but the court can refuse to help if the petitioner delayed unreasonably.

important_entities.name: Lex Fori (Law of the Forum)
important_entities.significance: The Law of Limitation is considered *Lex Fori* (the law of the court/forum where the case is filed). If two Indians sign a contract in France, and a breach happens, the limitation period to file a suit in an Indian court will be decided strictly by the Indian Limitation Act, not French law.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners will ask: 'If the defendant explicitly agrees to waive the defense of limitation in court, can the judge hear the time-barred case?' **NO**. Section 3 is absolute and touches the very jurisdiction of the court. The parties cannot mutually agree to bypass the Limitation Act. The court must dismiss it.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Use this keyword association to remember that equity and law only aid the watchful.

exam_strategy_tips: Whenever a Judiciary question asks 'Does the Law of Limitation extinguish the right or the remedy?', unconditionally select **Bars the Remedy, NOT the Right (except in Section 27)**.
